sections.heading: Algebraic Simplification
sections.html:
• To simplify, combine terms that have the same variable and exponent.

Q1. 2a+3b+5a−9b\text{Q1. }2a + 3b + 5a - 9bQ1. 2a+3b+5a−9b

Step 1: Group like terms as they have the same variable raised to the same power

  • (2a+5a)+(3b−9b)(2a+5a)+(3b-9b)(2a+5a)+(3b−9b)

Step 2: Simplify each group and write the simplified expression

  • 7a−6b\boxed{7a - 6b}7a−6b​

sections.heading: Algebraic Expansion
sections.html:
• When expanding products, multiply the values outside the brackets by the values inside the brackets.

Q1. 3x(2x−4y)\text{Q1. }3x(2x - 4y)Q1. 3x(2x−4y)

Step 1: Apply Distributive Law

  • a(b+c)=ab+aca(b+c) = ab + aca(b+c)=ab+ac
  • 3x(2x)+3x(−4y)3x(2x)+3x(-4y)3x(2x)+3x(−4y)

Step 2: Multiply each term inside by 3x

  • (3x)(2x)=6x2(3x)(2x) = 6x^2(3x)(2x)=6x2

  • (3x)(−4y)=−12xy(3x)(-4y) = -12xy(3x)(−4y)=−12xy

Step 3: Write the result

  • 6x2−12xy\boxed{6x^{2}-12xy}6x2−12xy​

Q2. (3x−5)(4x+8)\text{Q2. } (3x-5)(4x+8)Q2. (3x−5)(4x+8)
Step 1: Distribute 3x3x3x across the second bracket

  • 3x×4x=12x23x\times 4x = 12x^23x×4x=12x2

  • 3x×8=24x3x\times 8 = 24x3x×8=24x

Step 2: Distribute −5-5−5 across the second bracket

  • −5×4x=−20x-5\times 4x = -20x−5×4x=−20x

  • −5×8=−40-5\times 8 = -40−5×8=−40

Step 3: Combine all terms

  • 12x2+24x−20x−4012x^2 + 24x - 20x -4012x2+24x−20x−40

Step 4: Simplify like terms

  • 24x−20x=4x24x-20x = 4x24x−20x=4x

Step 5: Write the results

  • 12x2+4x−40\boxed{12x^{2}+4x-40}12x2+4x−40​

sections.heading: Algebraic Factorization
sections.html:
Q1. Factorize 12x2+18x\text{Q1. Factorize } 12x^2 + 18xQ1. Factorize 12x2+18x

Step 1: Find the HCF of the terms

  • HCF of coefficients 12 and 18 is 6.

  • HCF of variables x2x^2x2 and xxx is xxx.

  • Overall HCF is 6x6x6x

Step 2: Factor out the HCF

  • Write the HCF outside a bracket and divide each term by 6x6x6x.

  • 12x2÷6x=2x12x^{2}\div 6x = 2x12x2÷6x=2x, 18x÷6x=318x\div 6x = 318x÷6x=3

Step 3: Write the results

  • 6x(2x+3)\boxed{6x(2x+3)}6x(2x+3)​

sections.heading: Solving a Quadratic Equation
sections.html:
1. Factorization

  • Factorisation means rewriting the quadratic expression into two linear brackets. We look for two numbers that multiply to a×ca \times ca×c and add to b, then solve using the zero-product rule.

  • Worked Example

    Q1. Solve x2−x−6=0\text{Q1. Solve } x^{2}-x-6=0Q1. Solve x2−x−6=0

    Step 1: Identify the coefficients: a=1a=1a=1, b=−1b=-1b=−1, c=−6c=-6c=−6

    Step 2: Multiply a×c=1×(−6)=−6a \times c = 1 \times (-6) = -6a×c=1×(−6)=−6

    Step 3: Find two numbers that multiply to −6-6−6 and add to −1-1−1 →\rightarrow→ −3-3−3 and 222

    Step 4: Factorize: (x−3)(x+2)=0(x-3)(x+2)=0(x−3)(x+2)=0

    Step 5: Solve each bracket: x=3,−2x=3,-2x=3,−2

    Q2. Solve 2x2+7x+3=0\text{Q2. Solve } 2x^{2} + 7x + 3=0Q2. Solve 2x2+7x+3=0

    Step 1: Identify the coefficients: a=2a=2a=2, b=7b=7b=7, c=3c=3c=3

    Step 2: Multiply a×c=2×3=6a \times c = 2 \times 3 = 6a×c=2×3=6

    Step 3: Find the two terms that multiply to 6 and add to 7 →\rightarrow→ 666 and 111.

    Step 4: Rewrite: 2x2+6x+x+32x^{2}+6x+x+32x2+6x+x+3

    Step 5: Group Items: 2x(x+3)+1(x+3)2x(x+3)+1(x+3)2x(x+3)+1(x+3)

    Step 6: Factorize: (2x+1)(x+3)=0(2x+1)(x+3)=0(2x+1)(x+3)=0

    Step 7: Solve: x=−12,3x= \frac{-1}{2} , 3x=2−1​,3

  1. Quadratic Formula
x=−b±b2−4ac2a x = \frac{- b \pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4ac}}{2a} x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​
  • When the question says, “Give your answer to two decimal places,” use the formula!
  • Derivation of the Quadratic Formula is the same as saying “Make xxx the subject in ax2+bx+c=0ax^{2} + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0”
ax2+bx+c=0 ax^{2} + bx + c = 0 ax2+bx+c=0a(x2+bax)+c=0 a\left( x^{2} + \frac{b}{a}x \right) + c = 0 a(x2+ab​x)+c=0a((x+b2a)2−b24a2)+c=0 (Completing the Square) a\left( \left( x + \frac{b}{2a} \right)^{2} - \frac{b^{2}}{4a^{2}} \right) + c = 0 \text{ (Completing the Square)} a((x+2ab​)2−4a2b2​)+c=0 (Completing the Square)a(x+b2a)2−b24a+c=0 a\left( x + \frac{b}{2a} \right)^{2} - \frac{b^{2}}{4a} + c = 0 a(x+2ab​)2−4ab2​+c=0a(x+b2a)2=b2−4ac4a a\left( x + \frac{b}{2a} \right)^{2} = \frac{b^{2} - 4ac}{4a} a(x+2ab​)2=4ab2−4ac​(x+b2a)2=b2−4ac4a2 \left( x + \frac{b}{2a} \right)^{2} = \frac{b^{2} - 4ac}{4a^{2}} (x+2ab​)2=4a2b2−4ac​x+b2a=±b2−4ac4a2 x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm \sqrt{\frac{b^{2} - 4ac}{4a^{2}}} x+2ab​=±4a2b2−4ac​​x+b2a=±b2−4ac4a2 x + \frac{b}{2a} = \frac{\pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4ac}}{\sqrt{4a^{2}}} x+2ab​=4a2​±b2−4ac​​x+b2a=±b2−4ac2a x + \frac{b}{2a} = \frac{\pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4\text{ac}}}{2a} x+2ab​=2a±b2−4ac​​x=−b±b2−4ac2a x = \frac{- b \pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4\text{ac}}}{2a} x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​

  • Worked Example

    Q1. x2−x−6=0\text{Q1. }x^{2} - x - 6 = 0Q1. x2−x−6=0

    Step 1: Identify coefficients

    a=1a = 1a=1, b=−1b = - 1b=−1, c=−6c = - 6c=−6

    Step 2: Substitute in Formula

    x=−(−1)±(−1)2−4(1)(−6)2(1)x = \frac{- \left( - 1 \right) \pm \sqrt{\left( - 1 \right)^{2} - 4\left( 1 \right)\left( - 6 \right)}}{2\left( 1 \right)}x=2(1)−(−1)±(−1)2−4(1)(−6)​​

    Step 3: Simplify

    x=1±1+242=1±252x = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1+24}}{2} = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{25}}{2}x=21±1+24​​=21±25​​

    Step 4: Solve

    x=1+52=3 or x=1−52=−2x = \frac{1+5}{2} = 3 \text{ or } x = \frac{1-5}{2} = -2x=21+5​=3 or x=21−5​=−2

  1. Completing the Square

  • Completing the square is a method used to rewrite a quadratic expression of the form ax2+bx+cax^2+bx+cax2+bx+c into the form a(x+p)2+qa(x+p)^2+qa(x+p)2+q, which is useful for solving equations and finding the vertex of a parabola.

  • If an equation is in completing the square form, a(x+h)2+ka(x+h)^2+ka(x+h)2+k, the coordinates of the turning point (vertex) of the parabola are (−h,k)(-h,k)(−h,k)

  • Worked Example

    Q1. Solve x2+6x+5=0\text{Q1. Solve } x^{2} + 6x + 5 = 0Q1. Solve x2+6x+5=0

    Step 1: Identify the coefficients

    a=1a=1a=1, b=6b=6b=6, c=5c=5c=5

    Step 2: Take the half of the coefficient of xxx and square it

    Coefficient of xxx = 666

    Half of it = 62=3\frac{6}{2}=326​=3

    Square it = 32=93^{2}=932=9

    Step 3: Add and subtract this square inside the equation

    x2+6x+9−9+5x^{2}+6x+9-9+5x2+6x+9−9+5

    Step 4: Write as a perfect square

    (x2+6x+9)=(x+3)2(x^2 +6x+9) = (x+3)^{2}(x2+6x+9)=(x+3)2

    Step 5: Solve the equation

    (x+3)2−4=0(x+3)^{2}-4=0(x+3)2−4=0

    (x+3)2=4(x+3)^{2}=4(x+3)2=4

    x+3=±2x+3= \pm 2x+3=±2

    Step 6: Find the roots

    If x+3=2x+3=2x+3=2, then x=−1x=-1x=−1

    If x+3=−2x+3=-2x+3=−2, then x=−5x=-5x=−5

    Step 7: Write the final answer

    x=−1,−5\boxed{x=-1,-5}x=−1,−5​

  1. Graphing Method

  • Plot the graph of y=ax2+bx+cy=ax^2+bx+cy=ax2+bx+c

  • The points where the graph cuts the x-axis (y=0y=0y=0) are the solutions (roots) of the equation

sections.heading: Inequalities
sections.html:
• Solve like equations. Perform operations on both sides (add, subtract, multiply, divide) to isolate the variable.

  • When you multiply or divide by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign

  • Worked Examples

    Q1. Solve y−3≥−7\text{Q1. Solve }y-3 \geq -7Q1. Solve y−3≥−7

    Step 1: Add 3 to both sides

    y−3+3≥−7+3y-3+3 \geq -7+3y−3+3≥−7+3

    y≥4\boxed{y \geq 4}y≥4​

    Q2. Solve y−3≥−7\text{Q2. Solve } \frac{y}{- 3} \ge - 7Q2. Solve −3y​≥−7

    Step 1: Multiply both sides by -3

    Because you are multiplying by a negative, reverse the sign

    y≤−7×−3y \leq - 7 \times - 3y≤−7×−3

    Step 2: Simplify

    y≤21\boxed{y \leq 21}y≤21​

  • When two inequalities are present, split them into two

    Q1. Solve x<3x−1<2x+7\text{Q1. Solve }x < 3x - 1 < 2x + 7Q1. Solve x<3x−1<2x+7

    Step 1: Split into two inequalities

    Divide by -2, flip sign: x>12x > \frac{1}{2}x>21​

    2. 3x−1<2x+73x-1 < 2x+73x−1<2x+7

    x<8x<8x<8

    12<x<8\boxed{\frac{1}{2} < x < 8}21​<x<8​

sections.heading: Direct Proportion
sections.html:
• Two variables, xxx and yyy, are directly proportional if:
y∝x y \propto x y∝x
  • This means:
y=kx y = kx y=kx

  • where kkk is a non-zero constant, called the constant of proportionality.

  • As xxx increases, yyy increases and vice versa.

  • The ratio yx=k\frac{y}{x} = kxy​=k remains constant

sections.heading: Inverse Proportion
sections.html:
• Two variables, xxx and yyy, are inversely proportional if:
y∝1x y \propto \frac{1}{x} y∝x1​
  • This means:
y=kx y = \frac{k}{x} y=xk​

  • where kkk is a non-zero constant, called the constant of proportionality.

  • As xxx increases, yyy decreases and vice versa

  • The product xy=kxy = kxy=k remains constant.

sections.heading: Standard Form
sections.html: • y=ax3+bx2+cx+dy = ax^{3} + bx^{2} + cx + dy=ax3+bx2+cx+d

sections.heading: Key Properties
sections.html:
• The highest power of xxx is 3.
  • The graph can have:

    • Up to 2 turning points (maxima/minima).

    • One point of inflection (where gradient = 0, but curve doesn’t change direction)

  • The shape depends on the sign of aaa:

    • When a > 0, a min-max curve is formed

    • When a < 0 a max-min curve is formed

sections.heading: Turning Points
sections.html:
• Turning points are points on a graph where the gradient (slope) changes sign — the graph changes direction from increasing to decreasing, or vice versa

  • Found by differentiating:

dydx=3ax2+2bx+c \frac{dy}{dx} = 3ax^{2} + 2bx + c dxdy​=3ax2+2bx+c

and solving dydx=0\frac{dy}{dx} = 0dxdy​=0.

sections.heading: Standard Form
sections.html: • y=a(rx)+by = a(r^x) + by=a(rx)+b

sections.heading: Properties
sections.html:
1. Parameter aaa
  • Represents the vertical stretch and determines the initial value when x=0x=0x=0.
  1. Parameter rrr

  • Represents the base of the exponential function.

  • Determines whether the function is increasing or decreasing:

    • If r>1r > 1r>1, the curve increases as xxx increases

    • If 0<r<10 < r < 10<r<1, the curve decreases as xxx increases

  1. Parameter bbb

  • Represents the vertical shift of the graph

  • Shifts the curve upwards or downward

  • Determines the horizontal asymptote: y=by=by=b

  1. Asymptotes

  • A curve approaches but never touches these lines

  • For y=a(rx)+by=a(r^{x})+by=a(rx)+b, the asymptote is:

    y=by=by=b

  • There is no vertical asymptote, unless the domain is restricted

sections.heading: Gradient of a Curve
sections.html:
• For a straight line, the gradient is constant everywhere.
  • For a curve, the gradient changes at different points on the graph.

sections.heading: Method: Finding the Gradient at a Point (By Tangents)
sections.html:
1. Draw the graph

  2. Choose the point where you want to find the gradient

  3. Draw a tangent to the curve at that point, making sure it just touches the curve at that point (Use a ruler)

  4. Find the gradient of the tangent

Gradient=Change in yChange in x \text{Gradient} = \frac{\text{Change in }y}{\text{Change in }x} Gradient=Change in xChange in y​

sections.heading: Understanding Differentiation
sections.html:
• Differentiation finds the gradient (slope) of a curve at any point

  • It allows us to calculate the gradient of any xxx-coordinate on a curve.

sections.heading: Power Rule
sections.html:
• For function

    f(x)=xnf(x) = x^{n}f(x)=xn

  • The derivative is:

    ddx(xn)=n⋅xn−1\frac{d}{dx} (x^{n}) = n \cdot x^{n-1}dxd​(xn)=n⋅xn−1

  • Steps:

    1. Multiply by the exponent n

    2. Subtract 1 from the exponent

  • Worked Example

    ddx(x5)=5x4\frac{d}{dx} (x^{5}) = 5x^{4}dxd​(x5)=5x4

sections.heading: Differentiating Constants
sections.html:
• The graph is a horizontal line, so the gradient = 0.

  • ddx(a)=0\frac{d}{dx} (a) = 0dxd​(a)=0

sections.heading: Stationary Points
sections.html:
• A stationary point occurs where the gradient = 0

    dydx\frac{dy}{dx}dxdy​ = 0

  • Steps to find stationary points:

    1. Differentiate the function

    2. Set dydx\frac{dy}{dx}dxdy​ = 0

    3. Solve for xxx

sections.heading: Nature of Stationary Points
sections.html:
1. Second Derivative Test

  • Differentiate again to get d2ydx2\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}dx2d2y​

    • If d2ydx2>0\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} > 0dx2d2y​>0 →\rightarrow→ Minimum Point

    • If d2ydx2<0\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} < 0dx2d2y​<0 →\rightarrow→ Maximum Point

  1. Gradient Method

  • If the gradient changes +→−+ \rightarrow -+→−, the turning point is a Maximum

  • If the gradient changes from −→+- \rightarrow +−→+, the turning point is a Minimum

  1. Graph Shape Method

  • Look at the curve around the turning point:

    • If the curve is like a ∪\cup∪, it is a minimum.

    • If the curve is like a ∩\cap∩, it is a maximum.

sections.heading: Algebraic Indices
sections.html: • All the laws indices have been covered in the previous chapter. Here, we apply them to solve algebraic questions.

sections.heading: Worked Examples
sections.html:
Example 1

Q. Solve 32x=2\text{Q. Solve } 32^{x} = 2Q. Solve 32x=2

Step 1: Express both sides with the same base

We know: 32=2532 = 2^{5}32=25

32x=(25)x32^{x} = (2^{5} ) ^{x}32x=(25)x

Step 2: Apply the Power Rule

(25)x=25x(2^{5} )^{x} = 2^{5x}(25)x=25x

So, the equation becomes: 25x=212^{5x} = 2^{1}25x=21

Step 3: Use the One-to-One Property of Exponents

5x=15x = 15x=1

Step 4: Solve for xxx

x=15x= \frac{1}{5}x=51​

Final Answer: x=15\boxed{x = \frac{1}{5}}x=51​​

Example 2

Q. Simplify 3x−4×23x12\text{Q. Simplify } 3x^{-4} \times \frac{2}{3} x^{\frac{1}{2}}Q. Simplify 3x−4×32​x21​

Step 1: Group Constants and Variables

(3×23)×(x−4×x12)(3 \times \frac{2}{3} ) \times (x^{-4} \times x^{\frac{1}{2}} )(3×32​)×(x−4×x21​)

Step 2: Simplify Constants

3×23=23 \times \frac{2}{3} = 23×32​=2

Step 3: Apply the Product of Powers Rule

Use the law: xa×xb=xa+bx^{a} \times x^{b} = x^{a+b}xa×xb=xa+b

x−4×x12=x−4+12=x−72x^{-4} \times x^{ \frac{1}{2} } = x^{-4 + \frac{1}{2} } = x^{ \frac{-7}{2} }x−4×x21​=x−4+21​=x2−7​

Step 4: Combine Results

2×x−72=2x−722 \times x^{ \frac{-7}{2} } = 2x^{ \frac{-7}{2} }2×x2−7​=2x2−7​

Final Answer: 2x−72\boxed{2x^{ \frac{-7}{2} }}2x2−7​​

sections.heading: Elimination
sections.html:

Q. Solve {3x+2y=12 (Equation 1)2x−2y=4 (Equation 2)\text{Q. Solve } \begin{cases} 3x + 2y = 12 \text{ (Equation 1)} \\ 2x - 2y = 4 \text{ (Equation 2)} \end{cases}Q. Solve {3x+2y=12 (Equation 1)2x−2y=4 (Equation 2)​

(3x+2y)+(2x−2y)=12+4(3x+2y) + (2x-2y) = 12+4(3x+2y)+(2x−2y)=12+4

y=65y = \frac{6}{5}y=56​

sections.heading: Substitution
sections.html:
Example 1 (Linear - Linear)

Q. Solve {x+y=10 (Equation 1)2x−y=4 (Equation 2)\text{Q. Solve } \begin{cases} x + y = 10 \text{ (Equation 1)} \\ 2x - y = 4 \text{ (Equation 2)} \end{cases}Q. Solve {x+y=10 (Equation 1)2x−y=4 (Equation 2)​

Step 1: From Equation 1,

x=10−y (Equation 3)x = 10 - y \text{ (Equation 3)}x=10−y (Equation 3)

Step 2: Substitute into Equation 2

2(10−y)−y=42(10-y) -y =42(10−y)−y=4

20−2y−y=420 - 2y - y = 420−2y−y=4

20−3y=420 - 3y = 420−3y=4

3y=163y = 163y=16

y=163y = \frac{16}{3}y=316​

Step 3: Substitute y=163y = \frac{16}{3}y=316​ into Equation 3

x=10−163x = 10 - \frac{16}{3}x=10−316​

x=143x = \frac{14}{3}x=314​

Final Answer: (x,y)=(143,163)\boxed{ (x,y) = \left( \frac{14}{3} , \frac{16}{3} \right) }(x,y)=(314​,316​)​

Example 2 (Linear - Quadratic)

Q. Solve {y=x+1 (Equation 1)y=x2+3x (Equation 2)\text{Q. Solve } \begin{cases} y = x + 1 \text{ (Equation 1)} \\ y = x^{2} + 3x \text{ (Equation 2)} \end{cases}Q. Solve {y=x+1 (Equation 1)y=x2+3x (Equation 2)​

Step 1: Equate Equation 1 and Equation 2

x+1=x2+3xx + 1 = x^{2} + 3xx+1=x2+3x

Step 2: Rearrange

x2+3x−x−1=0 x^{2} +3x - x -1 = 0x2+3x−x−1=0

x2+2x−1=0x^{2} + 2x -1 =0x2+2x−1=0

Step 3: Solve the quadratic x=−2±22−4(1)(−1)2(1)x = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{2^{2} -4(1)(-1)} }{2(1)}x=2(1)−2±22−4(1)(−1)​​

x=−2±4+42x = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 4} }{2}x=2−2±4+4​​

x=−2±82x = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{8} }{2}x=2−2±8​​

x=−1±2x = -1 \pm \sqrt{2}x=−1±2​

Step 4: Find the corresponding yyy

  • If x=−1+2x = -1 + \sqrt{2}x=−1+2​:

    y=x+1=(−1+2)+1=2y = x + 1 = (-1 + \sqrt{2} ) +1 = \sqrt{2}y=x+1=(−1+2​)+1=2​

  • If x=−1−2x = -1 - \sqrt{2}x=−1−2​:

    y=x+1=(−1−2)+1=−2y = x + 1 = (-1 - \sqrt{2} ) +1 = - \sqrt{2}y=x+1=(−1−2​)+1=−2​

Final Answer: (x,y)=(−1+2,2) or (−1−2,−2)\boxed{ (x,y) = \left( -1 + \sqrt{2} , \sqrt{2} \right) \text{ or } \left( -1 - \sqrt{2} , - \sqrt{2} \right) }(x,y)=(−1+2​,2​) or (−1−2​,−2​)​

sections.heading: Graphical Method
sections.html:
• For linear + linear:

    • Plot both equations on the same axis

    • The solution is the point of intersection

    • If no solution →\rightarrow→ no solution

    • If lines overlap →\rightarrow→ infinitely many solutions

  • For linear + quadratic:

    • Intersection = line crosses the curve

    • Number of Intersections tells the number of solutions

sections.heading: Types of Inequalities in a Graph
sections.html:
• Strict Inequalities (<<<, >>>) →\rightarrow→ Use a broken/dashed line

  • Non-strict Inequalities (≤\leq≤, ≥\geq≥) →\rightarrow→ Use a solid line

sections.heading: Steps to Solve a Linear Programming Problem
sections.html:
• Write inequalities in the form y=mx+cy = mx + cy=mx+c
  • Draw straight-line graphs of each inequality
    • Use solid or broken lines depending on the inequality type
  • Test a point on either side of the line to see which side satisfies the inequality
  • Shade the required region for each inequality
    • The common area is called the feasible region

sections.heading: Introduction to Functions
sections.html:
• Functions are like pre-set rules: you input a value, apply the rule, and get an output.

  • Domain: The set of all possible input values (x-values) for a function.

  • Range: The set of all possible output values (y-values) from the function.

  • For an inverse, the domain and range are swapped

sections.heading: Inverse Function
sections.html:
Steps to find the Inverse Function f−1(x)f^{-1} (x)f−1(x)

  • Step 1: Replace f(x)f(x)f(x) with yyy: y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x)

  • Step 2: Swap xxx and yyy

  • Step 3: Solve for yyy in terms of xxx

  • Step 4: Replace yyy with f−1(x)f^{-1} (x)f−1(x)

    Example

    • f(x)=x2+9f(x) = x^2 + 9f(x)=x2+9

    • y=x2+9y = x^2 + 9y=x2+9

    • x=y2+9x = y^2 + 9x=y2+9

    • x−9=y2x-9 = y^2x−9=y2

    • y=±x−9y = \pm \sqrt{x-9}y=±x−9​

    • f−1(x)=±x−9f^{-1}(x) = \pm \sqrt{x-9}f−1(x)=±x−9​

sections.heading: Composite Function
sections.html:
• Notation: gf(x)=g(f(x))gf(x) = g(f(x))gf(x)=g(f(x))

Steps to Form a Composite Function

  • Step 1: Find f(x)

  • Step 2: Substitute f(x) into g(x)

  • Step 3: Simplify

  • Worked Example

    Find composite function {f(x)=3x−5g(x)=3(x+4)5\text{Find composite function } \begin{cases} f(x) = 3x - 5 \\ g(x) = \frac{3 (x+4) }{5} \end{cases}Find composite function {f(x)=3x−5g(x)=53(x+4)​​

    Step 1: Find f(x)f(x)f(x)

    f(x)=3x−5f(x) = 3x - 5f(x)=3x−5

    Step 2: Substitute into g(x)g(x)g(x)

    g(f(x))=3((3x−5)+4)5g(f(x)) = \frac{3 ( (3x - 5) + 4 )}{5}g(f(x))=53((3x−5)+4)​

    Step 3: Simplify

    g(f(x))=3(3x−1)5=9x−35g(f(x)) = \frac{3(3x - 1)}{5} = \frac{9x - 3}{5}g(f(x))=53(3x−1)​=59x−3​

    Final Answer: gf(x)=9x−35\boxed{ gf(x) = \frac{9x-3}{5} }gf(x)=59x−3​​

sections.heading: Distance-Time Graphs
sections.html:
• Speed=DistanceTime\text{Speed} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Time}}Speed=TimeDistance​

  • Average Speed=Total Distance TravelledTotal Time Taken\text{Average Speed} = \frac{\text{Total Distance Travelled}}{\text{Total Time Taken}}Average Speed=Total Time TakenTotal Distance Travelled​

  • From O to A: Uniform speed

    • Lines with a positive gradient represent objects moving away from the starting point

  • From A to B: Stationery (speed = 0)

    • Lines with a gradient of 0 represent the object to be at rest

  • From B to C: Uniform speed (return journey)

    • Lines with a negative gradient represent objects moving towards the starting point

  • Gradient of Distance - Time Graphs=Speed\text{Gradient of Distance - Time Graphs} = \text{Speed}Gradient of Distance - Time Graphs=Speed

sections.heading: Speed-Time Graphs
sections.html:
• From O to A: Uniform increase in speed
    • Lines with a positive gradient represent constant acceleration
  • From A to B: Constant speed (acceleration = 0)
    • Lines with 0 gradient represent constant speed
  • From B to C: Uniform deceleration/retardation
    • Lines with a negative gradient represent deceleration

  • Graph 1: A Straight Increasing Non-Horizontal Line indicates a constant acceleration where a > 0
  • Graph 2: Straight Decreasing Non-Horizontal Line indicates a constant acceleration where a < 0 or deceleration
  • Graph 3: Horizontal Line indicates moving at constant speed. a = 0
  • Gradient of Speed - Time Graph = Acceleration
  • If the acceleration is negative, it is called deceleration or retardation. (The moving body is slowing down.)
  • Acceleration=Change in VelocityTime=v−ut\text{Acceleration} = \frac{\text{Change in Velocity}}{\text{Time}} = \frac{v - u}{t}Acceleration=TimeChange in Velocity​=tv−u​

sections.html:
